editorial.headline: Where Pome and Stone Fruit Farming Fits in Indonesia’s KBLI Map
editorial.standfirst: This activity code covers the full farming cycle for apples, pears, plums, passion fruit, pomegranate and related pome and stone fruits.
editorial.body:
KBLI 01240 is a farming classification for pome and stone fruits: apples, apricots, cherries, peaches, nectarines, pears, quince, plums, sloe, passion fruit, kepel, tamarillo and pomegranate. Its scope is not merely the final harvest. The record describes a continuous agricultural chain, beginning with land preparation and planting, continuing through crop maintenance, and ending with harvesting and post-harvest work when those activities are performed as one integrated sequence. It also includes the cultivation of apple and stone-fruit plants for seed production.

That makes this a practical code for businesses whose centre of gravity is the cultivation of these fruit crops, including nursery and seedling activity tied to the same group of plants. A founder should read the scope as agricultural rather than trading, processing or hospitality-led: the defining activity is the preparation, growing, care, harvesting and post-harvest handling of the listed fruits. The language is broad enough to cover both familiar temperate names such as apple, pear, cherry and plum, and Indonesian-market crops such as markisa, kepel, terong Belanda and delima, provided the business is genuinely carrying out the farming cycle described in the record.

The scale picture is unusually open. The record lists Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar as open scales, so this classification is not reserved only for a large plantation operator. It can sit at micro and small scale, grow into a medium enterprise, or be registered at large scale where the business model and licensing profile justify it. For foreign investment, the national PMA status is also clear: TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the slim record does not show a foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity at the national level.

The Bali reading is also straightforward, and it matters because many agricultural categories can become more complicated once local registration practice is considered. Here, the record says the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and that the activity is not blocked by the Bali moratorium. The reason given is that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not caught by the province-wide rule that blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The honest conclusion is therefore clean: nationally, this is foreign-open up to 100%; in Bali, the record does not mark it as blocked for PMA registration under the stated moratorium.
